title: Two Pointers: Trapping Rain Water
oneLiner: Water above a bar is min(tallest to its left, tallest to its right) minus its height; two pointers find that min without extra arrays.
keyTakeaway: Water at i = min(maxLeft, maxRight) - height[i]. Start pointers at both ends and track leftMax and rightMax. Whichever side is LOWER is the bottleneck: its water level is already decided by its own max, because the other side is known to have something at least as tall. Settle that side, move it inward, repeat. O(n) time, O(1) space.
explanation:
An array gives the heights of bars of width 1. After it rains, how many units of water sit between them? For [0, 1, 0, 2, 1, 0, 1, 3, 2, 1, 2, 1] the answer is 6.

Look at a single position i. Water there rises until it would spill over the lower of the two walls around it: the tallest bar anywhere to its left and the tallest bar anywhere to its right. So water[i] = min(maxLeft[i], maxRight[i]) - height[i], counting the bar itself in both maxes so it is never negative. The straightforward solution precomputes both max arrays in two passes and sums. That is O(n) time and O(n) space, and a perfectly good first answer in an interview.

The two-pointer version drops the arrays. Put left at 0 and right at n - 1, and keep leftMax (tallest seen from the left so far) and rightMax. If height[left] < height[right], then the right side already has a bar taller than height[left], so for position left the limiting wall is leftMax, whatever lies in between. Update leftMax, add leftMax - height[left], and move left inward. Otherwise do the mirror image on the right. Each step settles one position for good, so the pointers meet after n - 1 steps.

Interviewers like this one because the greedy move needs a justification: say out loud why the lower side is safe to settle. Other answers they accept: the two max arrays above, or a monotonic stack that fills water layer by layer as it pops shorter bars. A common follow-up is the 2-D version (Trapping Rain Water II), which replaces the two pointers with a min-heap of boundary cells.

recognitionSignals: The answer at each position depends on the maximum to its LEFT and the maximum to its RIGHT (water, skyline, elevation profiles).
A first solution with two precomputed prefix/suffix arrays works, and the follow-up asks for O(1) extra space.
Two ends of an array can be processed independently as long as you always move the side that is "limited" -- the same move-the-smaller-side logic as Container With Most Water.
gotchas: Using only the max on one side (for example, a single left-to-right pass) overcounts water next to a tall left wall with a short right side.
Move the pointer on the LOWER side, not the higher one: only the lower side's water level is guaranteed by its own max.
Update the side's max before adding water, so a new tallest bar adds 0 rather than a negative amount. Empty and single-bar inputs trap 0.
confusableWith: Two Pointers: Two Sum on a Sorted Array (this track) also closes in from both ends, but decides which pointer to move by comparing a sum with a target; here you move whichever side has the lower bar.
Prefix Sums: Answer Range-Sum Queries in O(1) (this track) is the precompute-a-running-value idea behind the two max arrays; the two-pointer solution is what lets you skip storing them.

complexity.note: Each step settles one position and moves one pointer inward, so n - 1 steps; only two pointers and two running maxes are stored. (The two-max-arrays version is also O(n) time but O(n) space.)

referenceSolutions.python:
def trap(height):
    left, right = 0, len(height) - 1
    left_max = right_max = 0
    water = 0
    while left < right:
        # The lower side is the bottleneck, so its water level is already known.
        if height[left] < height[right]:
            left_max = max(left_max, height[left])
            water += left_max - height[left]
            left += 1
        else:
            right_max = max(right_max, height[right])
            water += right_max - height[right]
            right -= 1
    return water
